title: AI can diagnose you in seconds. But it comes with risks, doctors say
key_facts: Dr. Roshan Abid says that, with AI chatbots now widely available, she sees herself as 'doctor No. 3' after Google and a second doctor.
More people turn to apps such as ChatGPT Health and Claude for Healthcare before appointments, which is shaping how Nova Scotia physicians provide care.
Abid says AI often misses the critical thinking and patient context doctors apply, and that online information about GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic is often rife with misinformation.

Dr. Matthew Clarke, Nova Scotia Health's chief medical information officer, says patients often do not volunteer that they consulted AI, but that it has helped some consolidate their thoughts before seeing a doctor.
Nova Scotia physicians also use AI, for example to transcribe visits and to consult databases for tricky diagnoses; Clarke says strict, evolving rules govern doctors' use of AI.

Dr. Peter Lin of the Canadian Heart Research Centre says people entering health data into an AI platform consent to the company using it, that companies use it to train their systems, and that breaches are a risk.
Thousands of Nova Scotians have no family doctor, so many use AI to avoid emergency-room waits.
quote_evidence: Abid says that as more people turn to apps such as ChatGPT Health and Claude for Healthcare before their appointments, it is shaping the way Nova Scotia physicians provide care.
He says patients often will not volunteer that they have consulted AI out of fear of the stigma associated with the technology, but that it becomes apparent later where their perceptions originate.
He says even if companies strive for user privacy, the risk of bad actors and data breaches should always factor into decisions about submitting personal health information.
why_it_matters_hint: Doctors in one Canadian province say patients arrive with chatbot advice, some of it wrong, and that health data typed into a chatbot may be used to train it.
event_date: CBC article dated 10 Oct 2026; no single event
notes: Read CBC in full (CBC Nova Scotia reporter Ben Dornan). Anecdotal accounts from a few named doctors, no survey or usage figures.
